extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who practice before the USPTO (particularly trademark attorneys); respondents in OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Official USPTO disciplinary and professional-conduct standards governing practitioners who file and prosecute trademark matters before the Office, including signature rules, duties to clients, investigative cooperation, and sanctioning factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to act with reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are required to 'act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.' 'Reasonable ... when used in relation to conduct by a practitioner means the conduct of a reasonably prudent and competent practitioner.' Whether conduct is reasonable must be examined in the context of the surrounding circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner responsibilities include monitoring non-practitioner assistants to ensure their work complies with USPTO rules (including signature rules). Failure examples: relying on unsupported assumptions about firm procedures, failing to verify how client signatures were obtained, not asking to see filing receipts, not having or reviewing written procedures, and taking no steps to learn whether assistants impermissibly signed documents. Precedent: In re Mar; In re Lou.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep client reasonably informed and explain matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must 'keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter' and 'explain the matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a practitioner has notice that client filings may be affected by an issue (e.g., impermissible signatures), the practitioner must promptly notify clients and explain potential consequences and remedial options. Reliance on generic firm emails that do not describe the problem, consequences, or remedial steps is insufficient and may constitute a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements and permissible TEAS signature methods
rubrics_metrics.description: All trademark documents must be personally signed. TEAS signature methods include: (1) Direct Sign — individual enters his/her electronic signature (default); (2) ESIGN-ON — link sent to third party who electronically signs and uploads; (3) HSIGN-ON — pen-and-ink signature uploaded to TEAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must understand which signature method was used for filings they approve. It is impermissible for a person to sign another person's name on a TEAS form. Non-practitioner staff may assist in obtaining signatures but cannot themselves sign a client's name; the practitioner remains responsible for ensuring compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on signing another person's name and supervising non-practitioner assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not permissible for a person to sign another person's name to a TEAS form. Practitioners have the ultimate responsibility to ensure a client's affairs (including signature collection) are competently handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisory duties include instituting checks of assistants' work, verifying signature link emails or other evidence of client execution, and maintaining/consulting written procedures. Failure to supervise or to verify signature provenance can support a finding of misconduct under §§ 11.103 and 11.104. See In re Mar; In re Lou.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate with OED investigations and respond to RFIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) during investigations and respond to Requests for Information (RFIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation includes making reasonable inquiries of staff and clients as necessary to provide accurate, adequate answers to RFIs, seeking clarification from OED if needed, and not shifting blame to OED for failing to explain the basis of RFIs. Failure to meaningfully clarify confusion or to make reasonable inquiries undermines affirmative defenses and can support discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in OED disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision quotes a definition: evidence is 'clear' if certain, unambiguous, and plain to the understanding, and 'convincing' if reasonable and persuasive enough to cause the trier of fact to believe it (citing Foster v. AlliedSignal, Inc.). Practitioners asserting affirmative defenses bear the burden to prove them by clear and convincing evidence as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing discipline, consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the decision: aggravating factors included pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, and the practitioner's substantial practice in trademark law; a mitigating factor noted was the practitioner's long career. Sanctions should be supported by analysis of these factors (e.g., public reprimand and probation in this case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and disciplinary jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101–11.901; § 11.19(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct apply to persons who practice before the Office, and all practitioners engaged in practice before the Office are subject to the Office's disciplinary jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners appearing before the USPTO (including trademark attorneys) must comply with these rules; prior Codes applied before May 3, 2013. Discipline can include exclusion, suspension, reprimand, probation, and public notice to jurisdictions where practitioner is admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's review authority and procedural rights on appeal (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55, 11.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director reviews an ALJ's Initial Decision on the record and has authority to conduct a de novo review, and may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand the initial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rights include 20 days to request reconsideration under § 11.56(c) and the right to seek judicial review in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 (with applicable filing deadlines). The Director may also notify disciplinary agencies per § 11.59 of public discipline and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences to client rights and available remedies for improper signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper signatures on trademark filings may jeopardize the validity of registrations and could lead to cancellation unless remedial steps are taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible remedial actions include filing new declarations or ratifications; the decision cites TTAB and Commissioner precedent (In re Dermahose; In re Cowan) and TMEP § 611.01(b) indicating that failure to remediate may leave clients at risk. The mere theoretical availability of a harmless remedy is insufficient if the practitioner does not undertake remedial steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual assessment of 'reasonable' conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of 'reasonable diligence' or 'reasonableness' are fact-specific and must be evaluated in context rather than by categorical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing reasonableness considers available opportunities to discover issues (e.g., multiple RFIs, internal firm communications acknowledging widespread problems) and whether a reasonably prudent practitioner would have taken steps (personal inquiries, client notices, verification of signatures) under those circumstances.
